context.concept_name: Conceptual effect of sample size on confidence

coverage.learning_objective: Given two results with the same estimate but different sample sizes, explain why the estimate from the larger sample is more trustworthy.

required_facts.statement: A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample.

The more cases researchers observe, the more accurately they can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable on the response; in a single study, this is done by collecting a sufficiently large sample.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose two versions of the checkout-button test both come back showing the same 10% lift -- but one ran with 50 users in each group and the other ran with 5,000 users in each group. Should you trust them equally?

A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample. The more cases researchers observe, the more accurately they can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable (here, which button a user saw) on the response (whether they completed an order); in a single study, this is done by collecting a sufficiently large sample.

So the 5,000-user version of the checkout test tends to provide a more precise estimate of the button's effect than the 50-user version, even though both happened to show the same 10% lift -- the larger test observed far more cases, so it can estimate the button's effect on completed orders more accurately.

video_need.reason: The idea that small-sample estimates scatter more widely around the true effect than large-sample ones is a spread that's easier to picture with a diagram of estimates clustering tightly for the large sample and spreading widely for the small one than to hold in mind from a description alone.

practice_anchor.objective: Given two A/B tests on the same checkout-button change — one with 50 users per group and one with 5,000 users per group — both showing a 10% lift, explain in writing which result is more trustworthy and why, referencing precision of estimation and number of cases observed.
practice_anchor.success: The learner correctly identifies the 5,000-user test as more trustworthy, explains that a bigger sample provides a more precise point estimate, and states that observing more cases allows a more accurate estimate of the button's effect on completed orders.

visual_anchor.purpose: Side-by-side display of two groups of estimated lift values — one cluster tight around 10% (large sample) and one scattered widely around 10% (small sample) — making visible that small-sample estimates vary more around the true effect than large-sample ones.

context.concept_name: Conceptual interpretation of statistical significance/confidence level

coverage.learning_objective: Given a result reported with a significance or confidence figure, explain what that figure does and doesn't tell you about the underlying effect.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of "no difference", and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current data set, if the null hypothesis were true; it is used to quantify the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis.

Statistical significance is a measure of how unusual an experiment's results would be if there were actually no difference in performance between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to random chance alone.

A confidence interval represents a range of plausible values where we are likely to find the population parameter; if many samples were taken and a 95% confidence interval were built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain the parameter.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; such a difference is statistically significant but not practically significant.

misconceptions.statement: Not every confidence interval captures the true population proportion: in an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88), only one failed to contain the population proportion, showing that a small fraction of intervals will miss it even when the method is followed correctly.

teaching_blocks.content: The checkout test showed a 10% lift for the redesigned button. Before recommending it company-wide, you need language for how sure that result actually is.

The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of "no difference", and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration. For the checkout test, H0 would be that the redesigned button makes no real difference to completion rate, and HA would be that it does.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current data set, if the null hypothesis were true -- it quantifies the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis. Statistical significance measures how unusual a result would be if there were actually no difference between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to chance alone.

A confidence interval is a range of plausible values likely to contain the population parameter (the true value you are trying to estimate); if many samples were taken and a 95% interval built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain it.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval. So it's not quite right to say "there's a 95% chance the true completion-rate difference is in this interval" -- the 95% describes how the method behaves across many samples, not the probability attached to this one interval.

Not every confidence interval captures the true value, even when the method is followed correctly: in an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88), only one failed to contain the population proportion -- showing that a small fraction of intervals will miss it. The same is true of any single confidence interval you compute for a result like the checkout test.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; such a difference is statistically significant but not practically significant. A large enough checkout test could detect a tiny, practically unimportant lift and call it statistically significant -- significance tells you how unusual the result would be if there were truly no difference, not that the lift is big enough to matter.

video_need.reason: Hypotheses, p-values, and confidence intervals are all defined in terms of what would happen across many repeated samples -- an animation showing repeated samples each producing their own interval, most catching the true value and a few missing it, makes that repeated-sampling idea concrete in a way that a single static definition can't.

media.group_title: How p-values work and why a small p-value doesn't mean a large effect

segments.label: P-values, statistical significance, and the limits of a small p-value
segments.summary: Using a drug-comparison scenario, the clip builds up from a single-person trial to a large-sample experiment to show why we need many observations before drawing conclusions. It introduces the p-value as a way to quantify how confident we can be that two groups differ, explains the 0.05 threshold in terms of false positives (getting a significant result when there is actually no difference), and names the null hypothesis as the assumption that the two drugs are the same. It closes by showing that a larger sample can produce a smaller p-value for a one-point difference than a smaller sample produces for a six-point difference — demonstrating that a small p-value does not imply a large effect.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the false-positive framing explains the 0.05 threshold, and notice the final drug-sample comparison that shows effect size and p-value can move in opposite directions. The clip does not cover confidence intervals (f4, f5) or the misconception about interval capture (m1) — the text covers those.
bridge_note.after: The clip confirms that significance measures unusualness under no-difference, not the size of the effect. Confidence intervals, the repeated-sampling interpretation, and the interval-capture misconception are covered only in the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Given a result reported as 'significant at 95% confidence', write a plain-language explanation that correctly states what the confidence level means (how the method behaves across many samples) and explicitly rules out two common misreadings: that the result is practically important, and that there is a 95% probability the true value lies in this specific interval.
practice_anchor.success: The explanation correctly attributes the 95% to the long-run behaviour of the method, not to a probability attached to the single interval; it notes that statistical significance does not imply practical importance; and it does not claim the interval is guaranteed to contain the true value.

visual_anchor.purpose: A strip of twenty-five horizontal confidence intervals built from different samples around p = 0.88, with one interval visibly missing the true population proportion line — making the repeated-sampling interpretation and the interval-capture misconception concrete.

context.concept_name: Drawing a business conclusion from an experiment-result summary

coverage.learning_objective: Given an experiment's results, state a business conclusion that follows from the data without overreaching beyond what the numbers show.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested, and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration; the value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value.

In one hypothesis-test example, because the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample, that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

In a second example, the null value (p0 = 0.333) was not in the 95% confidence interval, so the null hypothesis was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; for example, an online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%, but this increase might not have any practical value.

While we failed to reject the null hypothesis in the first example, that does not necessarily mean the null hypothesis is true; perhaps there was an actual difference, but we were not able to detect it with the relatively small sample of 50.

misconceptions.statement: Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting the null hypothesis as true; it only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative.

teaching_blocks.content: Getting a p-value or confidence interval isn't the end of the job -- someone still has to decide what to do about the checkout button.

As before, H0 often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested, and HA an alternative claim under consideration; the value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value.

Consider two textbook examples, each testing whether a proportion equals a null value of 0.333. In one, because the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample, that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. In a second, the null value (p0 = 0.333) was not in the 95% confidence interval, so the null hypothesis was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.

While the first example failed to reject the null hypothesis, that does not necessarily mean the null hypothesis is true; perhaps there was an actual difference, but it could not be detected with the relatively small sample of 50. Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting the null hypothesis as true; it only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative.

Analyzing a test's results means saying whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect versus the baseline (control). For the checkout test, that means stating plainly whether the redesigned button did better, worse, or about the same as the original -- not just reporting a p-value and stopping. If the checkout test's summary showed its null value inside the confidence interval, the conclusion would be that the data did not provide sufficient evidence of a difference -- not that the new button makes no difference.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; for example, an online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%, but this increase might not have any practical value. A business conclusion has to weigh that: a statistically significant lift on the checkout button might still be too small to have any practical value, so look at the size of the lift, not just whether it was detected.

video_need.reason: The two contrasting outcomes -- a null value sitting inside a confidence interval versus falling outside it -- are easier to place and compare with a number-line diagram showing the interval and where the null value lands than to hold in mind from the worked numbers alone.

media.group_title: When statistical significance misleads: the sample-size effect

segments.label: Large samples can make trivially small differences statistically significant
segments.summary: The instructor explains that statistical significance is tightly linked to sample size: with n = 10, sample means of 10.05, 10.1, and 10.2 all produce large p-values and no evidence against the null; with n = 5,000 and identical sample means, the p-values become tiny and the same differences are called highly significant. The key point is that a tiny p-value only tells you the observed difference was unlikely under the null — it says nothing about whether a difference of 0.1 matters in practice. Whether the result has any practical importance is a separate question for domain experts.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the same three sample means flip from 'no evidence' to 'highly significant' just by changing n. The clip uses mu and box plots; Devspace's running example uses a proportion and a checkout button.
bridge_note.after: The clip covers f5 only. The text also covers the null-value/confidence-interval logic (f1–f3), the fail-to-reject misconception (f6, m1), and what a business conclusion must state (f4).

practice_anchor.objective: Given an A/B test summary card — showing the control conversion rate, the treatment conversion rate, the 95% confidence interval for the difference, and the null value — arrange the four reasoning steps in the correct order: (1) locate the null value relative to the confidence interval, (2) state the reject/fail-to-reject decision, (3) correct the fail-to-reject misconception if applicable, (4) write the plain-language business conclusion including whether the lift has practical value.
practice_anchor.success: The learner places all four steps in the correct sequence and writes a business conclusion that names the direction of the effect (or absence of evidence for one), does not claim the null is true when failing to reject, and flags whether a detected lift is large enough to matter practically.

visual_anchor.purpose: A number-line diagram showing a 95% confidence interval as a shaded band, with two scenarios side by side: one where the null value (p0 = 0.333) falls inside the interval (fail to reject) and one where it falls outside and below the interval (reject, conclude lower) — making the contrast between the two textbook examples immediately visible.

context.concept_name: Prioritizing findings by relevance to the stakeholder's specific decision, not by analytical interestingness

coverage.learning_objective: Prioritize which findings to lead with based on their relevance to the stakeholder's decision, rather than which finding is most analytically interesting.

required_facts.statement: The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions.
Crafting a communication's big idea requires knowing what is not essential, and boiling the overall message down to a single sentence that captures its core.
Writing about data should only include information relevant to the audience.
Use the inverted pyramid: the most important information should be first, and everything else arranged from most to least important.
source_refs: gov_uk_writing_about_data#Have a logical and organised structure

teaching_blocks.content: A full look into delivery times might turn up several findings -- Lagos slowed down, Kano's delivery times are the most variable, one courier has unusually fast times. Not all of them belong at the top of the report to the operations manager.

The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions -- and that decision (whether to add Lagos couriers) points to which finding matters most here: the Lagos slowdown, not the courier with the fastest times.

Crafting a communication's big idea requires knowing what is not essential, and boiling the overall message down to a single sentence that captures its core. Writing about data should only include information relevant to the audience -- the operations manager's decision about Lagos staffing doesn't need the full breakdown of every city's variability.

Use the inverted pyramid: the most important information should be first, and everything else arranged from most to least important -- so the Lagos finding opens the report, with the other findings following only if there's room and relevance for them.

video_need.reason: Ranking findings by relevance to a decision is a judgment call illustrated through the delivery-times scenario in prose, with no visual element.

practice_anchor.objective: Given five findings from a delivery-times analysis, choose and justify which two to lead a stakeholder summary with, based on relevance to the stated decision (whether to add Lagos couriers), not on analytical interestingness.
practice_anchor.success: The learner selects the two findings most directly tied to the Lagos staffing decision, places them first, and provides a one-sentence justification for each choice that references the stakeholder's decision rather than the finding's statistical novelty.

visual_anchor.purpose: A side-by-side display of five candidate findings, one column ordered by analytical interestingness and one ordered by relevance to the stakeholder's decision, making the contrast between the two ranking principles visible.

context.concept_name: Framing an actionable recommendation that is distinct from the finding itself

coverage.learning_objective: Frame a recommendation that states what action should be taken about a finding, distinct from restating the finding itself.

required_facts.statement: The value of analytical efforts is only truly realized when the insights discovered are acted upon; an audience cannot be assumed to find the intended takeaway as obvious as the presenter thinks it is.

In the example Big Idea '...was successful and, because of the success, we recommend continuing to offer it going forward; please approve our budget for this program.', it's clear to the audience what they need to know and what they are being asked to do.

teaching_blocks.content: "Lagos delivery times rose to 30 minutes" is a finding. "We recommend adding one more courier to the Lagos route" is something different: a recommendation, stating what should happen next.

The value of analytical efforts is only truly realized when the insights discovered are acted upon; an audience cannot be assumed to find the intended takeaway as obvious as the presenter thinks it is. Simply restating the Lagos finding again, more emphatically, may not tell the manager what to do about it -- the recommendation needs to say so explicitly.

In the example Big Idea "...was successful and, because of the success, we recommend continuing to offer it going forward; please approve our budget for this program," it's clear to the audience what they need to know and what they are being asked to do. "We recommend adding one Lagos courier; please approve the added headcount" does the same -- states the action and what's being asked of the reader.

video_need.reason: Distinguishing a recommendation from a restated finding is shown through one worked example in text, with no visual or procedural content.

practice_anchor.objective: Given the finding 'churn is highest in the first 30 days', write a distinct, actionable recommendation that states what action should be taken and what the reader is being asked to approve or do — without merely restating the finding.
practice_anchor.success: The learner's response names a concrete action (e.g. 'We recommend launching an onboarding check-in at day 14; please approve the added support resource') that is clearly distinct from the finding and includes an explicit ask, matching the pattern of the Big Idea example.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a finding statement alongside a correctly framed recommendation for the same situation, making the structural difference between restating data and stating an action visually obvious.

context.concept_name: Writing the context/setup for a findings narrative (why this analysis, what question it answers)

coverage.learning_objective: Write an opening context section for a findings narrative that establishes why the analysis was done, before presenting any finding.

required_facts.statement: In a story's structure, the beginning establishes the context: what's happening, or what the situation is, when the story begins.
A summary should have an obvious beginning, middle, and end; in one example the beginning level-sets the audience before diving into the analysis.

A release shouldn't start with lengthy background information or technical definitions; instead it should include a short paragraph explaining what the publication is about, with more detailed information placed in a separate section.
source_refs: gov_uk_writing_about_statistics_archived#Don’t start with lengthy background information or technical definitions

required_facts.statement: Explaining why the statistics have been collected includes relevant, factual information about the policy and operational context.
source_refs: gov_uk_writing_about_statistics_archived#Explain why the statistics have been collected

teaching_blocks.content: Before the operations manager reads any finding about Lagos delivery times, they need to know why they're reading this report at all.

In a story's structure, the beginning establishes the context: what's happening, or what the situation is, when the story begins. A summary should have an obvious beginning, middle, and end; in one example the beginning level-sets the audience before diving into the analysis.

A release shouldn't start with lengthy background information or technical definitions; instead it should include a short paragraph explaining what the publication is about, with more detailed information placed in a separate section. For the delivery report, that means a short opener -- "this report looks at delivery times across our three cities this month" -- rather than a page of methodology before getting to the point.

Explaining why the statistics have been collected includes relevant, factual information about the policy and operational context -- for instance, noting that this review was prompted by rising customer complaints about Lagos deliveries gives the reader a reason the analysis exists at all.

video_need.reason: Writing an opening context paragraph is a text-composition skill with a worked example; there is no visual mechanism to show.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a two-sentence context section introducing a findings report's purpose and question. The first sentence should state what the report covers and why the analysis was done; the second should name the specific question the analysis answers.
practice_anchor.success: The two sentences together establish what the report is about and why it exists, use no technical definitions or lengthy background, and give the reader a factual reason the analysis was conducted — all without referencing any finding or result.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a contrast between a weak opener that buries the purpose in lengthy background versus a strong two-sentence context section that immediately level-sets the reader on what the report covers and why it was done.

context.concept_name: Defining a capstone business question/problem statement

coverage.learning_objective: Define a specific business question or problem statement for a chosen dataset, so the question itself gives every later capstone step (retrieval, cleaning, analysis) a concrete target to serve.

required_facts.statement: Before analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified.
Scoping ensures an appropriate, common understanding of the problem is defined, and that expectations are aligned with what the analysis can produce.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the operations team at a courier company comes to you with a vague complaint: deliveries feel slow lately, can you look into it? That request isn't yet something you can analyze. Before any analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified.

Turning that complaint into a workable target is called scoping. Scoping ensures an appropriate, common understanding of the problem is defined, and that expectations are aligned with what the analysis can produce.

For the courier company, scoping the vague complaint means settling its context and boundaries: which orders (a specific quarter's deliveries), which measure (delivery time against a target), and which unit of comparison (delivery zone). The result is a specific business question: 'Which delivery zones are missing the delivery-time target, and by how much, over the last quarter?' That question already carries a context (this company's last quarter of orders) and boundaries (zones and delivery time, not every possible cause of delay), so you and the operations team share the same understanding of what the analysis will and won't answer.
Every later capstone step -- what data to retrieve, how to clean it, what to compute -- serves this one sentence. Scope it loosely, and the rest of the project has nothing precise to aim at.

video_need.reason: Turning a vague complaint into a specific, bounded question is a reasoning step, not a process with moving parts. A short recap slide of the before/after question is enough; the text already walks through the scoping itself.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a one-sentence business question or problem statement for a chosen capstone dataset, identifying the context (what data, what time period or scope) and the boundaries (what measure and unit of comparison the analysis will address).
practice_anchor.success: The sentence names a specific measurable question, states the context, and makes clear what the analysis will and will not answer — matching the scoping standard demonstrated in the courier-company example.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a vague complaint on the left ('deliveries feel slow lately') beside the scoped business question on the right ('Which delivery zones are missing the delivery-time target, and by how much, over the last quarter?'), with the three scoping decisions (which orders, which measure, which unit of comparison) annotated between them.

teaching_notes: Keep the delivery-operations scenario introduced here consistent for the rest of the capstone chunk.
Don't pre-empt the workflow-structure concept -- this block only scopes the question, not the whole project plan.

context.concept_name: Selecting an appropriate data retrieval method (SQL and/or spreadsheet)

coverage.learning_objective: Given the capstone dataset and where it is stored, choose and justify whether to retrieve it with a SQL query, a spreadsheet import, or both.

required_facts.statement: Data that lives in a SQL database can be retrieved with a SQL query; pandas' SQL query wrappers (pandas.io.sql) facilitate this retrieval.
read_excel() reads an Excel file directly into a DataFrame.

teaching_blocks.content: With the question scoped, the next decision is how to get the data. This capstone's order records live in the courier company's SQL database (an orders table), while the driver roster is kept in an Excel workbook.

Data that lives in a SQL database can be retrieved with a SQL query; pandas' SQL query wrappers (pandas.io.sql) facilitate this retrieval. So the orders table, sitting in the company's database, is a SQL-query job.
read_excel() reads an Excel file directly into a DataFrame. So the driver roster workbook, which never touches a database, is a read_excel() job instead.

The capstone ends up using both: a SQL query pulls the last quarter's orders (zone, driver_id, delivery_time) from the orders table, and read_excel() pulls the driver roster (driver_id, name, zone, shift) from the spreadsheet. Two different sources, matched to two different retrieval tools.

It can look like everything should go through one tool, but the method follows where each source actually sits: the orders table lives in the company's database, so a SQL query retrieves it, while the driver roster is an Excel workbook, so read_excel() reads it into a DataFrame.
Matching each source to its retrieval tool -- SQL query for the database, read_excel() for the workbook -- is the first executable step of the workflow, before any cleaning or analysis starts.

video_need.reason: Seeing both retrieval calls actually run against their real sources helps confirm the match, though the text's side-by-side explanation of database-vs-workbook already carries the decision.

context.concept_name: Structuring an end-to-end workflow (retrieval, cleaning, modeling, analysis, visualization, communication)

coverage.learning_objective: Sequence and structure the capstone's stages of retrieval, cleaning, modeling, analysis, visualization, and communication into an outline before starting execution.

required_facts.statement: An analytical project is commonly structured through phases that begin with scoping the question and end with delivering and communicating the results; a phase such as scoping or design may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations.

Within that structure, the source data is retrieved (for example via a SQL query or a spreadsheet import), and data quality should be assessed at every stage, with quality improvements (such as cleaning) focused as early as possible.
source_refs: uk_gov_data_quality_framework#3.1 Assess data quality at all stages of the lifecycle

required_facts.statement: Where the project's data spans more than one table, the modeling stage connects related tables; relationships are what connect related information between tables.

In the delivery and communication stage, insights are communicated to the commissioner and approver (the people who need them); activities may include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and presentations.

teaching_blocks.content: With the question scoped and both retrieval tools chosen, sketch the whole project's shape before touching either one.

An analytical project is commonly structured through phases that begin with scoping the question and end with delivering and communicating the results; a phase such as scoping or design may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations. For the capstone: scope the question, retrieve, clean/model, analyze, visualize, and communicate -- and if, say, cleaning the orders data reveals that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the source system, that sends you back to re-scope the question rather than pressing on.

Within that structure, the source data is retrieved (for example via a SQL query or a spreadsheet import), and data quality should be assessed at every stage, with quality improvements such as cleaning focused as early as possible. So right after the orders query and the roster import, the capstone checks for problems like missing delivery times, rather than waiting until the final analysis to discover them.

Where the project's data spans more than one table, the modeling stage connects related tables; relationships are what connect related information between tables. The capstone's orders and drivers are two such tables, so a modeling stage links them before any deeper analysis relies on both together.

In the delivery and communication stage, insights are communicated to the commissioner and approver -- the people who need them; activities may include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and presentations. The capstone's version of this is reporting the zone-delay findings back to the operations team that raised the original complaint.

Scope, retrieve, clean/model, analyze, visualize, communicate -- with quality checked throughout and any stage open to revisiting -- is the shape every remaining capstone concept fills in one piece at a time.

video_need.reason: Sequencing several phases, showing where a later phase can send you back to an earlier one, and connecting two tables mid-workflow are exactly the process relationships a diagram communicates better than prose alone.

practice_anchor.objective: Given the six named stages of the capstone workflow (scope, retrieve, clean/model, analyze, visualize, communicate), arrange them in the correct order and annotate each with: (a) what happens at that stage, (b) where quality should be assessed, and (c) which stage you would return to if a later stage revealed an ambiguity in the original question.
practice_anchor.success: The learner produces a correctly ordered six-stage outline, correctly places quality assessment as a continuous concern with cleaning focused early, correctly identifies the modeling stage as the point where multi-table relationships are connected, and correctly names the commissioner/approver as the audience for the communication stage — all without executing any SQL, pandas, or spreadsheet steps.

visual_anchor.purpose: A linear six-stage flow (Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model → Analyze → Visualize → Communicate) with a back-arrow from any later stage to Scope, a quality-check indicator spanning all stages, and a callout at the Model stage noting that relationships connect the orders and drivers tables.

teaching_notes: This concept only plans the sequence -- don't execute any of the SQL, pandas, or spreadsheet steps here, those are the next concepts.

context.concept_name: Independent, unassisted execution across multiple tool families

coverage.learning_objective: Independently carry out the capstone project's planned workflow across SQL, spreadsheet, Python/pandas, and visualization tools, without step-by-step guidance.

required_facts.statement: During the design phase, the commission is converted into an analytical plan, with some iteration expected as the solution is developed.

During the analysis phase, the planned analysis is carried out while progress and relevance are monitored, and appropriate records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained.

teaching_blocks.content: With the plan, retrieval, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and visualization steps all defined, what's left is carrying the whole thing out yourself, end to end, without being walked through each step again.

During the design phase, the commission is converted into an analytical plan, with some iteration expected as the solution is developed. For the capstone, the workflow outline from earlier becomes that analytical plan, and it's normal to adjust it once the SQL, spreadsheet, and pandas work actually starts.

During the analysis phase, the planned analysis is carried out while progress and relevance are monitored, and appropriate records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained. So as the capstone's query, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and figures get built, a short record of what was decided -- for example, how missing delivery times were handled -- is kept alongside a check that the results still answer the original zone-delay question.
Independent execution is running the whole plan yourself, adjusting it as needed, and keeping a record of the decisions made along the way -- not any single new tool.

video_need.reason: This concept is carrying out already-demonstrated tool work under one's own direction and keeping a decision record; there is no new mechanism, tool, or process a demo would add beyond restating the same two phases.

practice_anchor.objective: Complete the capstone project's execution independently against its plan, across the SQL, spreadsheet, and Python/pandas tools it requires, maintaining a decision record throughout.
practice_anchor.success: The learner submits a completed capstone artefact (queries, cleaned data, model, statistics, and figures) accompanied by a short decision log that records changes made to the original plan, how data-quality issues were handled, and a check that the outputs still answer the original analytical question — all produced without step-by-step guidance.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the two-phase structure (design → analysis) with an annotation at each phase indicating what is produced: an analytical plan (with iteration arrows) in the design phase, and a decision log alongside the analytical outputs in the analysis phase.

teaching_notes: TOC conflict: this concept's assessment_target mentions executing 'across SQL/spreadsheet/Python/BI', but the path teaches no BI-tool concept -- the text here covers only SQL, spreadsheet, and Python/pandas, the tools this capstone actually uses.

context.concept_name: Producing a stakeholder-facing narrated summary of the capstone

coverage.learning_objective: Write a narrated stakeholder summary that presents the capstone project's context, finding, and recommendation to its specific audience.

required_facts.statement: Designing a communication with a specific person in mind, even if that isn't always the reality, can help avoid treating a 'mixed audience' as one undifferentiated group; knowing what motivates that audience lets you frame what you need them to know or do in those terms.

During delivery, insights are communicated to the people who need them, sufficiently for them to determine whether the work meets their requirements; this communication can include summary packs, reports, or presentations.

A summary can follow a story structure with an obvious beginning, middle, and end: the beginning level-sets the audience with the big picture and background context, the middle presents what the analysis found, and the ending gives the key takeaway, such as a recommended next step.

teaching_blocks.content: The finished analysis now needs to be turned into something the operations team can act on: a narrated stakeholder summary of what was found.

Designing a communication with a specific person in mind, even if that isn't always the reality, can help avoid treating a 'mixed audience' as one undifferentiated group; knowing what motivates that audience lets you frame what you need them to know or do in those terms. So instead of writing for 'the ops team' in general, the capstone summary is written as if for the Head of Operations specifically, framing the zone-delay finding around what would motivate that person -- meeting the delivery-time target.

A summary can follow a story structure with an obvious beginning, middle, and end: the beginning level-sets the audience with the big picture and background context, the middle presents what the analysis found, and the ending gives the key takeaway, such as a recommended next step. For the capstone, that means opening with the courier company and last quarter's delivery-time target, then the finding that certain zones are missing it and by how much, then closing with a recommended next step -- though depending on the audience and relationship, that recommendation can instead be placed up front for a Head of Operations who prefers the bottom line first.

During delivery, insights are communicated to the people who need them, sufficiently for them to determine whether the work meets their requirements; this communication can include summary packs, reports, or presentations. For the capstone, that means the finished summary pack should let the Head of Operations judge for themselves whether it actually answers the zone-delay question they raised, not just report that the analysis was done.
A narrated summary aimed at one specific person, moving through beginning, middle, and end, is what turns the capstone's findings into something its audience can actually use.

video_need.reason: Writing for a specific audience and following a beginning/middle/end story structure is a composition skill the worked example already walks through in full; a short recap of the structure is enough.

practice_anchor.objective: Write the narrated stakeholder summary that concludes the capstone project: a short written document addressed to the Head of Operations that opens with the business context and delivery-time target, presents the zone-delay finding with its key numbers, and closes with a recommended next step — framed around what motivates that audience.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted summary has a clear beginning (business context and target), middle (specific zone-delay finding with numbers), and end (a recommended next step); it is addressed to a named audience role and frames the finding in terms that audience cares about; it does not include unexplained technical detail.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a raw analytical finding (e.g. a table of zone delay percentages) alongside the finished narrated summary paragraph, so the learner can see how the same information is transformed into an audience-facing story with context, finding, and recommendation.

teaching_notes: Applies already-learned audience-framing and story-structure skills to the capstone's own findings -- keep the recap of those skills short, the point is the capstone's own summary.

context.concept_name: Documenting and presenting the finished capstone deliverable

coverage.learning_objective: Produce documentation and a presentation of the finished capstone deliverable that lets someone else understand and evaluate the work without having watched it get built.

required_facts.statement: Transparency about the analytical decisions, process, limitations, and changes made at each stage should be clearly shown through documentation of the analysis, assumptions, and data, together with records of the decisions and quality-assurance checks made.
Delivery and communication activities can include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and giving presentations.

teaching_blocks.content: The very last capstone step: package the finished work so someone who never watched it get built can understand and evaluate it.

Transparency about the analytical decisions, process, limitations, and changes made at each stage should be clearly shown through documentation of the analysis, assumptions, and data, together with records of the decisions and quality-assurance checks made. For the capstone, that means documenting things like how missing delivery-time values were handled, what 'last quarter' was defined as, and the checks run to confirm the Orders/Drivers keys matched correctly.

Delivery and communication activities can include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and giving presentations. The capstone's deliverable is the finished report or summary pack, together with the visualization set already built, presented to the operations team that raised the original question.

Documenting the decisions made and presenting the finished report and visuals together is what makes the capstone a deliverable someone else can evaluate, rather than just finished work only you understand.

video_need.reason: Writing up decisions and assembling the already-built report and visuals into a presentation is a documentation task, not a new mechanism or tool a demo would clarify.

practice_anchor.objective: Write up and present the finished capstone project as a polished deliverable: produce a documentation section that records the key analytical decisions, assumptions, data-handling choices, and quality-assurance checks made at each stage, then assemble the finished report or summary pack together with the visualization set and present it to a non-technical audience.
practice_anchor.success: The submission includes a documentation section that explicitly records at least three analytical decisions or assumptions (e.g. how missing values were handled, how a time period was defined, how a join key was verified), and a completed summary pack or report that pairs the visualization set with a plain-language narrative addressed to the stakeholder who raised the original question.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the two-part structure of the final capstone step: (1) a documentation layer capturing decisions, assumptions, and QA checks at each prior stage, feeding into (2) a delivery layer comprising the summary pack, visualizations, and presentation — making clear that both parts together constitute the evaluable deliverable.

teaching_notes: This concept packages work already done in earlier capstone concepts -- don't re-explain the SQL, pandas, or visualization steps themselves, only how they get documented and presented.

clusters.title: Sample Size, Effect Size, and Statistical Significance
clusters.reasoning: Sample size/effect size and statistical significance/confidence intervals are two interconnected statistical concepts for evaluating experiment validity. Sample size determines whether an effect can be detected; significance tells you whether the detected effect is likely real. They are always interpreted together and form one idea: 'is this result trustworthy?' Business conclusions from experiments are the translation step that applies these concepts to a decision, and are better shown separately.

clusters.title: Prioritizing Findings and Framing Recommendations
clusters.reasoning: Prioritizing findings by relevance (selecting which results matter most to the stakeholder) and framing recommendations as actionable (stating what to do, not just what was found) are two aspects of the same editorial decision: what to lead with and how to say it. Narrative context setup is about structuring the opening of a presentation, which is a distinct communication skill.

clusters.title: Defining the Question and Planning the Workflow
clusters.reasoning: Defining the business question, selecting the data retrieval method, and structuring the end-to-end workflow are three sequential planning steps for a capstone project. They form one idea: scoping and planning an analysis before executing it. A learner cannot choose a retrieval method without a defined question, and cannot structure the workflow without knowing both.

clusters.title: Narrating and Delivering the Capstone
clusters.reasoning: The narrated stakeholder summary and the documented/presented deliverable are two forms of the same final output: communicating the capstone results. The narration is the verbal presentation; the documentation is the written artifact. They read as two aspects of one idea: delivering the completed analysis to a stakeholder. Independent execution is the process of doing the work, which is a distinct concept.
